I PREFACE The Provincial Cabinet of Coins was formed in 1904. Its inclusion in the following year amongst the collections benefited in the distribution of treasure trove is responsibe for its acquisition of the greater niuni>er of the coins which are now catalogu(*d. In 1909 the ( kuiiicil of the Asia-

tic Society of Bengal presented to the Cabinet a selection of coins from the duplicates discovc'red in the process of cataloguing their collection along with that of the Indian Museum. The association of Assam with Eastern Bengal between the years 190r> and 1912 led to the (\abin(‘l's securing some interesting finds of Bengal coins froih the Dac^ca and Mymeiisingh districts, and valuable finds of coins of this class have also lieen made in 8ylhet and Nowgong. The Cabinet (‘onsequently now' possesses a very rejiresentative collection of some of the liengal (governors and Kings. The chief strength of the Cabinet, however, naturally lies in the class of Assam (a>iiis. An appeal to local officers when the Cabinet was first formed only produced about tliirty of these coins in addition to a small collection of iwentj^-two present- ed by Munshi Muhammad Shah of Jorhat. In 1906, how'cver, a find of nearly a thousand coins, mainly of the Ahom Kings, occurred on the Daflating Tea Carden in Sibsagar. As Deputy Commissioner of that district from 1906 to 1909 the present editor was able to purchase a number of coins for the Cabinet, and in 1914 eighty-five more Assamese coins were purchased from a private collector of the same district. A selection of Manipur coins was presented by the Manipur Darbar in 1908, and a inimber of I®bch coins by His High- ness the Maharaja of Cooch Behar in 1909. The small but interesting collection of the rare Kaehari coinage was pur-

chased in the North Cachar Hills in 1912. viii preface. The first catalogue of the collection, which was publish- ed in 1911 and described about 600 coins, was prepared under the supervision of Mr. H. E. Stapleton, Indian Edu- cational Service, who was then Honorary Secretary to the Coin Committee, Eastern Bengal and Assam. A supple- ment containing the description of nearly 1,300 addi- tional coins was brought out by Mr. R. Friel, i.c.s. and the present editor in 1919. Since then a large number of coins has been added to the Cabinet and the preparation of a new and complete edition of the Catalogue is overdue. The number of coins now catalogued is over 4,000. Brief introductory historical and descriptive remarks on the several classes of coins were included in the first edition of the catalogue. Their purpose will now be better served by a reference to that admirable little book “The Coins of India’ (The Heritage of India Series) by C. J. Brown, (1922), and they have accordingly been omitted from the present edition, except in the case of the Assam sections, the strength and local importance of which .call for a more detailed account than can be expected from that work. In dealing with the Bengal coins Part I of Mr. H. E. Stapleton’s ‘‘ contributions to the History and Ethnology of North-Eastern India ” which appeared in J. A. S. B. XVIII,

1922, has been found most helpful ; and the edition has to thank Mr. Staple ton for allow ing him to use also certain notes com- piled with a view to later and as yet unpublished parts of the same work. 443 ASSAM COINS^ Section XXXIV. THE XHOM kings OF ASSAM. The founders of the Ahom kingdom were Shans, who in 1228 a.d. crossed the Patkoi range, which bounds the Brahmaputra Valley- at the extreme east, and settled in the neighbourhood of the modern Sibsagar. For about 300 years they remained a unit among the several tribes that then inhabited the Brahma* putra Valley, but about 1530 -a.d., under the leadership of SuhunmuA, they succeeded in finally conquering their principal rivals, the Chutiyas and Kacharis, and were brought into intimate contact with the world outside the Assam A^alley by an unsuccessful invasion of the Muhammadans, who then ruled over Eastern Bengal. Their success evidently inspired them to imitate the coinage of the Muhammadan Rings of the Husaini dynasty, and in 1543 the first Ahom coin was issued by ^ukletimun, the son of Ruhutimuii. This coin has an ins- cription in the Ahom language and script, and, following a statement made in the Yogini Tantra that the Ahom country was octagonal, the coins are q^tagonal instead of round ; but in other respects they follow closely coins of Nastat BhAh and Obyasuddin, two of Al&-ud-din Husen Shah’s sons. The progress ai the Ahoms towards Hinduism is reflected in the Sanskrit inscriptions (in the |A.8sa- mese or Bengali character) on two coins of Jayadhvaja and Chakradhyaja. The earlier coins, with the exception of those of ^uklehmuA bear the dates of accession of the kings who issued them. Rudra Sitfsha, 1696 — 1714' A.D., introduced an annual issue from 1696 (1618 Sdka), and specimens of coinage in the Assamese script are known for nearly every year until the end of the

Ahom rule in 1821 (1743 Sdka), Even after the introduction of the annual coinage, however, the old association of coinage with the king’s aooession was maintained, at any rate in the case of certain kings, by the issue of coins in the old Ahom character in the first year of the reign. All the full coins are on the same lines, the obverse containing the name of the king and the date of the coin, while the reverse contains an expression of the king’s devotion to particular deities. The form of the inscription appears .to have^ 29 448 XHOM kings of ASSAM. been borrowed directly from the coins struck by the Bengal Hindu kings Danu- jamarddana and Mahendra Deva in the 15th century. The most interesting coins of the series are those minted in the name of Siva Sitiiha^and KAje&vara Simha. The former king permitted his wives to strike coins on his behalf, and in 1661 S6ha his queen Pramathefevari for the first time broke away from the Assamese tradition by striking at Garhgaon a square coin in Persian script. The shape of this coin may have been derived from the square Manipuri coins, issued shortly before by Chairomba. Riijesvara experimented in new forms of coinage almost throughout his reign. Besides ordinary octagonal coins in Ben- gali script, he struck in the first year of his reign octagonal coins in Ahom script (vide coin at bottom of Plate VII) and square coins in Bengali script were also issued. Besides these, he issued octagonal coins with a Nagari inscription in 1675 S6]ca and at least two issues of coins in Persian were also struck, — a square issue in 1674 Sdlca and an octagonal issue in 1685. On both the latter coins the name of the mint, Rangpur, is mentioned.

Towards the end of Assamese rule, the Vaishnava section of the inhabitants of Assam constantly broke out into rebellion against their kings, who were fol- lowers of Siva. 1x1 the time of Gaurin^tha Simha two Vaishnava usurpers began to strike coins in Upper Assam, and the Assamese kingdom was only saved from immediate dissolution by the temporary intervention of the British in 1794 A.D. Owing to the adoption of a policy of non-intervention, the British soon withdrew, and for nearly 30 years anarchy prevailed. Towards the end of this period, invasions of Burmese occurred, and the last King of Assam, Jogedvara Simha was a puppet of the Burmese Governors. The last dated coin known is a quarter-rupee of Jogesvara minted in 1743 Sakd (1821 a.o.) The aggressions of the Burmese finally led to a British expedition for the purpose of ejecting them from Assam and Manipur. Rangpur was occupied at the beginning of 1825 a.d., and by the treaty of Yandabo, signed on February the 24th, 1826, the Burmese King undertook to have no further dealings with Assam. Owing to the atrocities perpetrated by the Burmese, Assam had fallen into a most deplorable condition, and the administration of the country was entirely conducted for several years after the treaty by British officials. An attempt to reinstate Purandara Simha, who had previously reigned for a short time in 1816 ^.d., ended in failure, and from 1838 Assam has formed an integral part of British India. The progenitor of the Koch Kings is said to have been a Mech or Koch named Haria Mandal, a resident of Chikangram in the district of Goalpara, and the recognized head of twelve leading families of Meches (or Koches) living in the Khuntaghat pargana. He married the two daughters of one Haju, and had two sons, Bisu and Sisu. The Muhammadans under Husen Shah conquered the local kingdom of Kamata about 1493, but retained no permanent hold on the country. After their departure it was divided amongst numerous petty chiefs, of whom Bisu was one. Ultimately, about 1516 a.d., Bisu succeeded in conquering his neighbours, and, being then converted to Hinduism, he assumed the name of Bisva Siiiiha, and removed his capital from Chikangram to the present site of Kuch Bihar. He died about 1540 a.d. At the time of his death, his two eldest sons, Malla Deva and Sukladhvaj, were away at Ben- ares, and their brother, Nara Sirhha, taking advantage of their absence, pro- claimed himself king. As soon as the news reached Malla Deva and Sukladh- vaj, they hastened home and defeated Kara Sirfiha, who fled to Nepal and

finally Kashmir. Malla Deva then ascended the throne under the name of Nara N»rfiyana, Sukladhvaj (nicknamed Silarai, King of the Kites, from his rapidity of movement in warfare) being appointed the commander-in-chief. The Koch power reached its zenith during the reign of Nara Niirsyana, and his conquests are said to have extended over the whole of the Assam Valley, the Khasi and Jaintia Hills, Manipur, Tipperah, and part of Sylhet. When Viryavanta, the Chief of the Khiram State on the Khasi Hills, tendered his submission voluntarily, the Buranjis state that a condition imposed on him was that his coins should, in future, be struck in the name of Nara N^rtfyana, with the sign of a mace as a distinguishing mark from those of the Koch king’s own mint. Specimens of these latter coins, however, have not yet been found, and the Khasi chiefs have no record that their predecessors ever struck coins of their own. 4 , Finally, however, Nara NdrAyana himself succumbed in 1668 to an invasion by K^ls Rih<r, the famous general of the Bengal Sultan Sulaimfin Kararfini. Silarai was taken prisoner and carried to Gaur, but was later released and returned home. Nara Nlriiyana probably regained his independence whilst the Pathan Sultans of Bengal were being subjugated by the Emperor Akbai, THE KOCH KINGS. 525 Nara Ndriiyana did not marry till late in life, when he had a soh Lakshml Niirdyana. Up to then, Silarai’s son, Raghu Deva, had been rl^arded as hia heir, and after Silarai’s death Raghu Deva quarrelled with his uncle and waa allowed in 1581 to set up a subordinate kingdom in the area east of the San- kosh, undertaking to strike coins only in his uncle’s name. On Nara Nr»r6-

yana’s death, probably in 1587, Lakshmf NarAyana succeeded him in the western part of the kingdom and struck coins dated 1609 saka (1587 a.d.), whilst Raghu Deva declared his independence and struck coins in his own nanie in the following year. Neither of the Koch kingdoms long retained its independence. Lakshmi Niiniyana declared himself a vassal of the Mughal Emperor in 1696, mainly apparently with the object of obtaining assistance against his cousin. This object was attained and Raghu Deva’s son Parikahit was defeated in 1612 or 1613 by a Mughal force. Lnkshmi Nar.iyana and his descendants continued to reign in the western kingdom, which later became known as Kuch Bihar, but only as vassals of the Mughal Empire. The right of miming full rupees was denied to them, and henceforth their coinage consisted only of the curious half rupees with incomplete inscriptions which are known as “ Narriyani rupees.’^ The only known exceptions are two or three full coins of Prana Nfiriyana in the British Museum, which bear the saha date 1566 (1633 A.D.). These were probably struck during the period between 1658 and 1662 when Priina Nilrayana is known to have made a bid for independence. The date on the coins probably represents the date of PrAna NArayana’s accession, and tlie coins may be re- garded as a claim to indi'pendent status “ with retrospective effect.” The eastern Koch kingdom, or Koch Hajo, ceased to exist as an inde- pendent kingdom with the defeat of Parikshit. Its territory was a bone of con- tention between the Muhammadans and the Ahoms until 1638 when the Bar Nadi was accepted as the boundary between the two powers. The descend- ants of Raghu Deva administered a tract as subordinates of tlie Ahon' but had no right of coinage. The only known coins of the eastern Koch king-

dom are a very few rupees of Ragliu Deva, one of them being in this Cabinet, and a sinjgle rupee of Parikshit in the collection of the author. The Koch rupees closely follow the model of one of the coins of Hus6n of Bengal. The inscriptions are Sanskrit, in an archaic Bengali script, and are on similar lines to those of the Ahom coins. The half-rupees are struck from dies much larger than the coins, and the inscriptions are therefore incomplete. The copper half- coins included in this section are unintelligently executed copies of the Koch half-rupees, and are probably Bhutan copies of those coins. 536 LIST OF KOCH KINGS. S. -86. Section XXXVII. THE KINGS OF JAINTIAPUR. Within historical times the dominions of the Rajas of Jaintiapur extended over the tract in the plains of Sylhet now known as the Jaintia parganas, in which their capital Jaintiapur was situated, and the adjacent hill area, known as the Jaintia Hills and inhabited by the Synteng branch of the Khasis, which was the original home of the dynasty. The inhabitants of the Jaintia parganas preserve in their traditions a list of kings of whom the seventh, Dhan Manik, is known to have been reigning at the close of the sixteenth century. The first of the list bears the name of Parbat Ray, “ Lord of the Hills ”, and it seems probable that he was the >Synteng chief wh(j first extended his sway over the plains tract, perhaps early in the sixteenth century. Hardly anything however is known of the history of the earlier rulers except the occasional record in the Koch and Ahom annals of their conflicts with the Koches, Ahoms and Kachans. The records of the Koch kings state that in the middle of the sixteenth century Silarai, brother of the Koch King Nara Narayana, defeated and slow the Raja of Jaintia and imposed on his son the condition that ho should not issue coins in his own name. An inscription on the gateway of the ruined palace at Jain- tiapur states that it was erected by Lakshmi Narayana, who ruled at the end of the seventeenth century. The Jaintia Rajas maintained a precarious indepen- dence until 1835, when their territory was annexed by the British in conse- quence of the sacrifice of three British subjects to the goddess Kali. The rupees of the Jaintia kings, like those of the Koch kings, werelnodei- led on coins of the Husaini dynasty of Bengal. The inscription is on the same

lines as those on the Koch coins, except that the issuing ruler was described merely as “ the Lord of Jaintiaimr ” and not by name, owing, according to tradition, to the stipulation imposed by Silarai. Coins are known bearing the aaka dates 1591, 1592, 1630, 1653, 1696, 1704, 1707 and 1712 (A. D. 1669, 1670, 1708, 1731, 1774, 1782, 1785 and 1790), and it may fairly be assumed that as in the case of the Koch and e^irlier Ahom coins, these dates represent the dates of accession (or perhaps of the installation) of the kings who issued the coins. Quarter rupees dated 1653 and 1712 aaka bear the names of Bar Gosain and RAm Simha respectively, the stipulation imposed by Silarai being apparently regarded as applying only to the coinage of full coins. KINGS OF JAINTIAPUR. 543 The rupees are locally known as katra taka (sword rupees) from the fact that they bear the device of a two-handed sword and a musket on them. They are made, particularly those of later date, of debased metal, doubtless a result of the system under which the right to mint coin was sold by auction to the highest bidder. It is unfortunate that the small collection of Jaintia rupees which was described by Sir Edward Gait in J. A. S. B. S. 1 15. Section XXXVIII. MANIPUR. Mackenzie writes as follows in his North-East Frontier (page 1491). — “ The early history of Manipur was barbarous in the extreme. It was not only mark- ed by constant raids of the Manipuris into Burma and of the Burmese into Manipur, but by internal wars of the most savage and revolting type, in which sons murdered fathers, and brothers murdered brothers, without a single trait of heroism to relieve the dark scene of blood and treachery.” The modern history of the State begins from the time (1709 A.D.?) when Pamheiba (or Oha- rib Niwaz, as he was called subsequently) shot his adopted father and occupied the throne. The records of Manipur contain a list of chiefs, given below for what it is worth, going back to the first century of the (Christian era, but many of these earlier chiefs are probably entirely legendry. The Shillong Cabinet has been singularly unfortunate as regards Manipur coins, as two collections have been lost in transit. The few coins catalogued below belong to the series locally known as Set or “ Shell ” coins, and are com- posed of bell-metal, obtained chiefly from Burma. They are small in size, weighing 8 to 18 grains, and varying in market value from 400 to 450 to a Bri- tish rupee. The process of mintage consisted in the metal being first cast in little pellets, which were then softened by fire. The pellets were next flat- tened by a blow of the hammer into an irregularly rounded figure, and stamped by a punch with a letter cut on it (said to be the initial letter of the regnant king’s name). There is no evidence of there having been at any time a gold coinage in existence ; but Prinsep states that a square silver coinage existed

from at least 1712 A.D. A square coin of Chaurjit dated 1734 aaka, which is in the possession of Mr. Stapleton, weighs 173 grains. About seven years prior to 1873 A.D. an attempt was made by the then Political Agent to intro- duce the ordinary Indian copper coinage, and a large number of pice were sup- plied by Government. The experiment, however, resulted in total failure, as the women in the bazars refused to accept them. Since the British expedi- tion of 1891, however, the indigenous coinage has ceased to be current except in the more out-of-the-way parts of the State, the ordinary English coins of silver and copper being used instead. Square copper coins of larger size and of greater weight are also known to have been in use in Manipur. MANIPUR STATE. LIST OF RAJAS OF MANIPUR. From State records. 549 Years. :l. 443 ASSAM COINS^ Section XXXIV. THE XHOM kings OF ASSAM. The founders of the Ahom kingdom were Shans, who in 1228 a.d. crossed the Patkoi range, which bounds the Brahmaputra Valley- at the extreme east, and settled in the neighbourhood of the modern Sibsagar. For about 300 years they remained a unit among the several tribes that then inhabited the Brahma* putra Valley, but about 1530 -a.d., under the leadership of SuhunmuA, they succeeded in finally conquering their principal rivals, the Chutiyas and Kacharis, and were brought into intimate contact with the world outside the Assam A^alley by an unsuccessful invasion of the Muhammadans, who then ruled over Eastern Bengal. Their success evidently inspired them to imitate the coinage of the Muhammadan Rings of the Husaini dynasty, and in 1543 the first Ahom coin was issued by ^ukletimun, the son of Ruhutimuii. This coin has an ins- cription in the Ahom language and script, and, following a statement made in the Yogini Tantra that the Ahom country was octagonal, the coins are q^tagonal instead of round ; but in other respects they follow closely coins of Nastat BhAh and Obyasuddin, two of Al&-ud-din Husen Shah’s sons. The progress ai the Ahoms towards Hinduism is reflected in the Sanskrit inscriptions (in the |A.8sa- mese or Bengali character) on two coins of Jayadhvaja and Chakradhyaja. The earlier coins, with the exception of those of ^uklehmuA bear the dates of accession of the kings who issued them. Rudra Sitfsha, 1696 — 1714' A.D., introduced an annual issue from 1696 (1618 Sdka), and specimens of coinage in the Assamese script are known for nearly every year until the end of the

Ahom rule in 1821 (1743 Sdka), Even after the introduction of the annual coinage, however, the old association of coinage with the king’s aooession was maintained, at any rate in the case of certain kings, by the issue of coins in the old Ahom character in the first year of the reign. All the full coins are on the same lines, the obverse containing the name of the king and the date of the coin, while the reverse contains an expression of the king’s devotion to particular deities. The form of the inscription appears .to have^ 29 448 XHOM kings of ASSAM. been borrowed directly from the coins struck by the Bengal Hindu kings Danu- jamarddana and Mahendra Deva in the 15th century. The most interesting coins of the series are those minted in the name of Siva Sitiiha^and KAje&vara Simha. The former king permitted his wives to strike coins on his behalf, and in 1661 S6ha his queen Pramathefevari for the first time broke away from the Assamese tradition by striking at Garhgaon a square coin in Persian script. The shape of this coin may have been derived from the square Manipuri coins, issued shortly before by Chairomba. Riijesvara experimented in new forms of coinage almost throughout his reign. Besides ordinary octagonal coins in Ben- gali script, he struck in the first year of his reign octagonal coins in Ahom script (vide coin at bottom of Plate VII) and square coins in Bengali script were also issued. Besides these, he issued octagonal coins with a Nagari inscription in 1675 S6]ca and at least two issues of coins in Persian were also struck, — a square issue in 1674 Sdlca and an octagonal issue in 1685. On both the latter coins the name of the mint, Rangpur, is mentioned.

Towards the end of Assamese rule, the Vaishnava section of the inhabitants of Assam constantly broke out into rebellion against their kings, who were fol- lowers of Siva. 1x1 the time of Gaurin^tha Simha two Vaishnava usurpers began to strike coins in Upper Assam, and the Assamese kingdom was only saved from immediate dissolution by the temporary intervention of the British in 1794 A.D. Owing to the adoption of a policy of non-intervention, the British soon withdrew, and for nearly 30 years anarchy prevailed. Towards the end of this period, invasions of Burmese occurred, and the last King of Assam, Jogedvara Simha was a puppet of the Burmese Governors. The last dated coin known is a quarter-rupee of Jogesvara minted in 1743 Sakd (1821 a.o.) The aggressions of the Burmese finally led to a British expedition for the purpose of ejecting them from Assam and Manipur. Rangpur was occupied at the beginning of 1825 a.d., and by the treaty of Yandabo, signed on February the 24th, 1826, the Burmese King undertook to have no further dealings with Assam. Owing to the atrocities perpetrated by the Burmese, Assam had fallen into a most deplorable condition, and the administration of the country was entirely conducted for several years after the treaty by British officials. An attempt to reinstate Purandara Simha, who had previously reigned for a short time in 1816 ^.d., ended in failure, and from 1838 Assam has formed an integral part of British India. The progenitor of the Koch Kings is said to have been a Mech or Koch named Haria Mandal, a resident of Chikangram in the district of Goalpara, and the recognized head of twelve leading families of Meches (or Koches) living in the Khuntaghat pargana. He married the two daughters of one Haju, and had two sons, Bisu and Sisu. The Muhammadans under Husen Shah conquered the local kingdom of Kamata about 1493, but retained no permanent hold on the country. After their departure it was divided amongst numerous petty chiefs, of whom Bisu was one. Ultimately, about 1516 a.d., Bisu succeeded in conquering his neighbours, and, being then converted to Hinduism, he assumed the name of Bisva Siiiiha, and removed his capital from Chikangram to the present site of Kuch Bihar. He died about 1540 a.d. At the time of his death, his two eldest sons, Malla Deva and Sukladhvaj, were away at Ben- ares, and their brother, Nara Sirhha, taking advantage of their absence, pro- claimed himself king. As soon as the news reached Malla Deva and Sukladh- vaj, they hastened home and defeated Kara Sirfiha, who fled to Nepal and

finally Kashmir. Malla Deva then ascended the throne under the name of Nara N»rfiyana, Sukladhvaj (nicknamed Silarai, King of the Kites, from his rapidity of movement in warfare) being appointed the commander-in-chief. The Koch power reached its zenith during the reign of Nara Niirsyana, and his conquests are said to have extended over the whole of the Assam Valley, the Khasi and Jaintia Hills, Manipur, Tipperah, and part of Sylhet. When Viryavanta, the Chief of the Khiram State on the Khasi Hills, tendered his submission voluntarily, the Buranjis state that a condition imposed on him was that his coins should, in future, be struck in the name of Nara N^rtfyana, with the sign of a mace as a distinguishing mark from those of the Koch king’s own mint. Specimens of these latter coins, however, have not yet been found, and the Khasi chiefs have no record that their predecessors ever struck coins of their own. 4 , Finally, however, Nara NdrAyana himself succumbed in 1668 to an invasion by K^ls Rih<r, the famous general of the Bengal Sultan Sulaimfin Kararfini. Silarai was taken prisoner and carried to Gaur, but was later released and returned home. Nara Nlriiyana probably regained his independence whilst the Pathan Sultans of Bengal were being subjugated by the Emperor Akbai, THE KOCH KINGS. 525 Nara Ndriiyana did not marry till late in life, when he had a soh Lakshml Niirdyana. Up to then, Silarai’s son, Raghu Deva, had been rl^arded as hia heir, and after Silarai’s death Raghu Deva quarrelled with his uncle and waa allowed in 1581 to set up a subordinate kingdom in the area east of the San- kosh, undertaking to strike coins only in his uncle’s name. yana’s death, probably in 1587, Lakshmf NarAyana succeeded him in the western part of the kingdom and struck coins dated 1609 saka (1587 a.d.), whilst Raghu Deva declared his independence and struck coins in his own nanie in the following year. Neither of the Koch kingdoms long retained its independence. Lakshmi Niiniyana declared himself a vassal of the Mughal Emperor in 1696, mainly apparently with the object of obtaining assistance against his cousin. This object was attained and Raghu Deva’s son Parikahit was defeated in 1612 or 1613 by a Mughal force. Lnkshmi Nar.iyana and his descendants continued to reign in the western kingdom, which later became known as Kuch Bihar, but only as vassals of the Mughal Empire. The right of miming full rupees was denied to them, and henceforth their coinage consisted only of the curious half rupees with incomplete inscriptions which are known as “ Narriyani rupees.’^ The only known exceptions are two or three full coins of Prana Nfiriyana in the British Museum, which bear the saha date 1566 (1633 A.D.). These were probably struck during the period between 1658 and 1662 when Priina Nilrayana is known to have made a bid for independence. The date on the coins probably represents the date of PrAna NArayana’s accession, and tlie coins may be re- garded as a claim to indi'pendent status “ with retrospective effect.” The eastern Koch kingdom, or Koch Hajo, ceased to exist as an inde- pendent kingdom with the defeat of Parikshit. Its territory was a bone of con- tention between the Muhammadans and the Ahoms until 1638 when the Bar Nadi was accepted as the boundary between the two powers. The descend- ants of Raghu Deva administered a tract as subordinates of tlie Ahon' but had no right of coinage. The only known coins of the eastern Koch king-

dom are a very few rupees of Ragliu Deva, one of them being in this Cabinet, and a sinjgle rupee of Parikshit in the collection of the author. The Koch rupees closely follow the model of one of the coins of Hus6n of Bengal. The inscriptions are Sanskrit, in an archaic Bengali script, and are on similar lines to those of the Ahom coins. The half-rupees are struck from dies much larger than the coins, and the inscriptions are therefore incomplete. The copper half- coins included in this section are unintelligently executed copies of the Koch half-rupees, and are probably Bhutan copies of those coins. 536 LIST OF KOCH KINGS. S. -86. Section XXXVII. THE KINGS OF JAINTIAPUR. Within historical times the dominions of the Rajas of Jaintiapur extended over the tract in the plains of Sylhet now known as the Jaintia parganas, in which their capital Jaintiapur was situated, and the adjacent hill area, known as the Jaintia Hills and inhabited by the Synteng branch of the Khasis, which was the original home of the dynasty. The inhabitants of the Jaintia parganas preserve in their traditions a list of kings of whom the seventh, Dhan Manik, is known to have been reigning at the close of the sixteenth century. The first of the list bears the name of Parbat Ray, “ Lord of the Hills ”, and it seems probable that he was the >Synteng chief wh(j first extended his sway over the plains tract, perhaps early in the sixteenth century. Hardly anything however is known of the history of the earlier rulers except the occasional record in the Koch and Ahom annals of their conflicts with the Koches, Ahoms and Kachans. The records of the Koch kings state that in the middle of the sixteenth century Silarai, brother of the Koch King Nara Narayana, defeated and slow the Raja of Jaintia and imposed on his son the condition that ho should not issue coins in his own name. An inscription on the gateway of the ruined palace at Jain- tiapur states that it was erected by Lakshmi Narayana, who ruled at the end of the seventeenth century. The Jaintia Rajas maintained a precarious indepen- dence until 1835, when their territory was annexed by the British in conse- quence of the sacrifice of three British subjects to the goddess Kali. The rupees of the Jaintia kings, like those of the Koch kings, werelnodei- led on coins of the Husaini dynasty of Bengal. The inscription is on the same

lines as those on the Koch coins, except that the issuing ruler was described merely as “ the Lord of Jaintiaimr ” and not by name, owing, according to tradition, to the stipulation imposed by Silarai. Coins are known bearing the aaka dates 1591, 1592, 1630, 1653, 1696, 1704, 1707 and 1712 (A. D. 1669, 1670, 1708, 1731, 1774, 1782, 1785 and 1790), and it may fairly be assumed that as in the case of the Koch and e^irlier Ahom coins, these dates represent the dates of accession (or perhaps of the installation) of the kings who issued the coins. Quarter rupees dated 1653 and 1712 aaka bear the names of Bar Gosain and RAm Simha respectively, the stipulation imposed by Silarai being apparently regarded as applying only to the coinage of full coins. KINGS OF JAINTIAPUR. 543 The rupees are locally known as katra taka (sword rupees) from the fact that they bear the device of a two-handed sword and a musket on them. They are made, particularly those of later date, of debased metal, doubtless a result of the system under which the right to mint coin was sold by auction to the highest bidder. It is unfortunate that the small collection of Jaintia rupees which was described by Sir Edward Gait in J. A. S. B. No. 3, 1895, as having been purchas- ed for the Asiatic Society of Bengal, and which contained certain coins, including the two quarter coins mentioned above, of wh;ch there is no other i*ocord, was not forthcoming when the Society’s collection was catalogued along with that of the Indian Museum. 35 LIST OF KINGS OF JAINTIA. S. 1 15. Section XXXVIII. MANIPUR. Mackenzie writes as follows in his North-East Frontier (page 1491). — “ The early history of Manipur was barbarous in the extreme. It was not only mark- ed by constant raids of the Manipuris into Burma and of the Burmese into Manipur, but by internal wars of the most savage and revolting type, in which sons murdered fathers, and brothers murdered brothers, without a single trait of heroism to relieve the dark scene of blood and treachery.” The modern history of the State begins from the time (1709 A.D.?) when Pamheiba (or Oha- rib Niwaz, as he was called subsequently) shot his adopted father and occupied the throne. The records of Manipur contain a list of chiefs, given below for what it is worth, going back to the first century of the (Christian era, but many of these earlier chiefs are probably entirely legendry. The Shillong Cabinet has been singularly unfortunate as regards Manipur coins, as two collections have been lost in transit. The few coins catalogued below belong to the series locally known as Set or “ Shell ” coins, and are com- posed of bell-metal, obtained chiefly from Burma. They are small in size, weighing 8 to 18 grains, and varying in market value from 400 to 450 to a Bri- tish rupee. The process of mintage consisted in the metal being first cast in little pellets, which were then softened by fire. The pellets were next flat- tened by a blow of the hammer into an irregularly rounded figure, and stamped by a punch with a letter cut on it (said to be the initial letter of the regnant king’s name). There is no evidence of there having been at any time a gold coinage in existence ; but Prinsep states that a square silver coinage existed

from at least 1712 A.D. A square coin of Chaurjit dated 1734 aaka, which is in the possession of Mr. Stapleton, weighs 173 grains. About seven years prior to 1873 A.D. an attempt was made by the then Political Agent to intro- duce the ordinary Indian copper coinage, and a large number of pice were sup- plied by Government. The experiment, however, resulted in total failure, as the women in the bazars refused to accept them. Since the British expedi- tion of 1891, however, the indigenous coinage has ceased to be current except in the more out-of-the-way parts of the State, the ordinary English coins of silver and copper being used instead. Square copper coins of larger size and of greater weight are also known to have been in use in Manipur. MANIPUR STATE. LIST OF RAJAS OF MANIPUR. From State records. 549 Years. :l.
